issues.legal_issue: The pre-constitutional cessation of a periodically payable allowance does not bar a constitutional writ claim where each later missed payment is a fresh deprivation and the dispute remains under consideration.
material_facts: The grants had been converted into money allowances payable at regular intervals.
Payments were stopped before the Constitution came into force, but the grantees continued corresponding with the government about their claims until the dispute was treated as final.
issues.conclusion: The preliminary objection that the claims could not be brought because the allowances were stopped before the Constitution came into force was overruled.
issues.legal_principle: A periodically payable allowance gives rise to a fresh claim when a periodic payment is withheld. The Court relied on the recurring nature of the deprivation and the continuing correspondence between the parties.

rule.if: constitutional_writ_case and recurring_allowance and periodic_nonpayment and correspondence_pending

predicates.constitutional_writ_case: The claimant brings a constitutional writ proceeding to enforce a claimed right.
predicates.recurring_allowance: The claimed benefit is an allowance payable periodically at regular intervals.
predicates.periodic_nonpayment: The government withholds one or more periodic payments of the allowance.
predicates.correspondence_pending: The claimant continues seeking reconsideration of the withheld allowance from the government.

issues.definition: When a constitutional writ case concerns a periodically payable allowance, missed periodic payments, and continuing correspondence about the claim, the pre-constitutional timing of the initial stoppage does not bar the proceeding.

issues.legal_issue: A court may determine whether a new sovereign has recognized a right arising under the former sovereign, and a right so recognized may be enforced in the new sovereign’s courts.
material_facts: The former ruler granted a maintenance allowance to a family member under the former state's rules.
An order made by the new sovereign continued the prior laws, including rules, regulations, and orders based on custom or usage, until they were altered or amended.
The former state's rules governing the grant were not displaced by an applicable enactment, and the allowance continued until the government stopped it.
issues.conclusion: The new sovereign recognized the grant through the order continuing the former state's laws, so the grantee's right was enforceable; the act-of-state objection did not prevent the court from determining whether recognition had occurred.
issues.legal_principle: An act of state is the acquisition of sovereignty over territory by conquest, treaty, cession, or otherwise. Municipal courts cannot review the propriety or legality of that acquisition or enforce unrecognized pre-existing rights. They may, however, determine whether the new sovereign recognized a claimed right expressly or by implication, including through its legislation or conduct; the claimant bears the burden of proving recognition. The Court relied on Secretary of State of India v. Kamachee Boye Sahaba, Cook v. Sprigg, Secretary of State for India v. Bai Rajbai, Vajesingji Joravarsingji v. Secretary of State for India in Council, Dattatraya Krishna Rao Kane v. Secretary of State for India, Secretary of State v. Sardar Rustam Khan, State of Saurashtra v. Memon Haji Ismail Haji, Jagannath Agarwala v. State of Orissa, Thakur Amar Singhji v. State of Rajasthan, and Madharao Phalke v. State of Madhya Bharat. It also relied on the continuing-law order and Article 327 of the Constitution.

rule.if: act_of_state_rights_dispute and former_sovereign_grant and new_sovereign_preserved_prior_law and claimant_proved_recognition

predicates.act_of_state_rights_dispute: The proceeding concerns a claim to enforce a right created under a former sovereign after sovereignty over the territory has changed.
predicates.former_sovereign_grant: The former sovereign granted the claimant a right under the former state's law or practice.
predicates.new_sovereign_preserved_prior_law: The new sovereign continued the former state's relevant law or rules until they were altered or amended.
predicates.claimant_proved_recognition: The claimant establishes that the new sovereign recognized the claimed right expressly or through its legislation or conduct.

issues.definition: A former-sovereign grant may be enforced in an act-of-state rights dispute when the new sovereign preserved the relevant prior law and the claimant proves recognition of the right.

issues.legal_issue: A government cannot use general extra-territorial administrative powers or a validating provision to annul a right preserved by an order made under the governing law-making provision.
material_facts: The prior state's rules governing the maintenance grant continued under an order made by the government exercising delegated authority.
The government stopped the allowance by an executive decision rather than by a further order under the provision authorizing orders to alter or amend the continued law.
The government relied on general authority to exercise extra-provincial jurisdiction and on a provision validating acts done in that jurisdiction.
issues.conclusion: The executive annulment was unauthorized, and the government was directed to continue the allowance from when it had been withheld.
issues.legal_principle: The Extra Provincial Jurisdiction Act, 1947, sections 3(1), 4, and 5, must be read harmoniously. Section 3(1) does not override section 4, and a valid order made under section 4 may be superseded only by another order under that section. Section 5 validates acts done in the exercise of extra-provincial jurisdiction but does not authorize abrogation of laws continued under section 4 or an order made under it. The Court relied on the Administration of Orissa States Order, 1948, paragraph 4(b), and the Extra Provincial Jurisdiction Act, 1947.

predicates.extra_provincial_administration_case: The dispute concerns government administration of territory outside a province under delegated extra-provincial authority.
predicates.prior_law_preserved: An operative order continued the former state's relevant law or rules until they were altered or amended by a competent order.
predicates.executive_stopped_grant_without_competen: The government stopped a grant by executive action without making a competent order under the authority governing alteration of the continued law.

issues.definition: In an extra-provincial administration case, an executive stoppage of a grant is unauthorized when the relevant prior law was preserved and no competent amending order was made.

issues.legal_issue: An annulment order made under the statutory authority governing extra-provincial administration has the effect of law and cannot be reviewed merely for its propriety or fairness when it is not alleged to be beyond that authority.
material_facts: The grantee held grants made by a former ruler before the territory was administered by the new sovereign.
A competent government made an order under the statutory provision authorizing orders for the administration of the territory, expressly annulling the commitments that included those grants.
The grantee did not contend that the annulment order was beyond the authority conferred by that provision.
issues.conclusion: The order had the effect of law and validly terminated the claimed rights; the court could not investigate whether the annulment was proper or just.
issues.legal_principle: An order made under section 4 of the Extra Provincial Jurisdiction Act, 1947, has legislative effect. Where the order is not challenged as ultra vires, its propriety or fairness is not a matter for the court to investigate. The Court relied on section 4 of that Act.

rule.if: extra_provincial_order_challenge and former_ruler_grant and competent_statutory_annulment_order and no_ultra_vires_challenge

predicates.extra_provincial_order_challenge: The proceeding challenges an order made in the administration of territory under extra-provincial authority.
predicates.former_ruler_grant: The claimant relies on a grant made by a ruler before the change in sovereignty.
predicates.competent_statutory_annulment_order: A competent government made an order under the statutory authority for administration of the territory that expressly annulled the grant.
predicates.no_ultra_vires_challenge: The claimant does not contend that the annulment order exceeded the authority under which it was made.

issues.definition: A former-ruler grant is validly terminated when a competent statutory annulment order expressly ends it and the claimant does not challenge that order as beyond authority.

issues.legal_issue: A maintenance allowance recognized and implemented by the new government cannot be ended by a mere executive fiat.
material_facts: The new government modified a former ruler's maintenance grant and recognized an allowance at a reduced rate.
The government paid the recognized allowance over a period of time.
The allowance was later stopped following a statement by the Chief Minister, without a further order having the effect of law.
issues.conclusion: The recognized right remained intact, and the grantee was entitled to a declaration and a writ requiring the government to perform its obligation.
issues.legal_principle: Recognition of a former ruler's grant, followed by implementation through payment, makes the recognized right enforceable against the new government; it cannot be abrogated by a mere executive fiat. The Court applied the principles governing recognition of rights by a new sovereign and distinguished a legislative order from executive action.

rule.if: challenge_to_executive_termination and new_government_recognized_allowance and government_paid_allowance and termination_by_executive_fiat

predicates.challenge_to_executive_termination: The proceeding challenges the government's termination of a maintenance allowance by executive action.
predicates.new_government_recognized_allowance: The new government expressly recognized or modified the claimant's allowance.
predicates.government_paid_allowance: The government implemented the recognized allowance by making payments to the claimant.
predicates.termination_by_executive_fiat: The government stopped the allowance through an executive decision rather than a legally effective order.

issues.definition: A recognized and paid allowance remains enforceable when the government ends it only by executive fiat.

issues.legal_issue: The property protection in section 299(1) of the Government of India Act, 1935, does not create or enlarge an enforceable right that the new sovereign has not recognized.
material_facts: A grantee relied on section 299(1) to argue that a grant made by a former ruler could not be taken away without authority of law.
The Court's prevailing conclusion in the relevant petition rested on recognition of the grant under the new sovereign's order.
Two judges stated that the property protection would not assist a grantee whose right had not been recognized by the new sovereign.
issues.conclusion: Section 299(1) protects only rights the grantee had when becoming a citizen of the Dominion; it does not enlarge rights or cure an infirmity in them. This statement was made in the separate opinion of two judges.
issues.legal_principle: Section 299(1) of the Government of India Act, 1935, protects existing property rights but does not create or enlarge a right against a new sovereign; recognition by the new sovereign is necessary for a former ruler's grantee to establish the right in the new sovereign's courts. The two judges relied on State of Gujarat v. Jamadar Mahomed Abdulla.

predicates.former_ruler_property_claim: The claimant seeks to enforce a property right originating in a grant made by a former ruler.
predicates.claimant_became_subject_of_new_sovereign: The claimant became a citizen or subject of the new sovereign after sovereignty changed.
predicates.new_sovereign_did_not_recognize_right: The new sovereign did not recognize the claimant's asserted right expressly or by implication.

issues.definition: A former ruler's grantee who becomes a subject of a new sovereign cannot rely on property protection to create an enforceable right if the new sovereign did not recognize that right.
